evidence: Ter. Ad. 254: beneficium accipere (Lewis & Short, as Ad. 2.3.1)
terms.comment: A service one was free not to render; one owed by family or by station is an officium (Sen. Ben. 3.18.1, quoted by Lewis & Short). beneficium dare, accipere, reddere; beneficiō tuō, thanks to you.
The polite request of Cicero’s letters: grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī …, “you will do me the greatest favour if …”. A plain “please” is sī mē amās (Cic. Fam. 9.20.3).
A kindness done for someone who has a claim to it, as a friend or kinsman has (Lewis & Short); its other common sense is duty.

evidence: Plaut. Capt. 3.5.63: ab eō petītō grātiam istam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare in this sense (Lewis & Short); its everyday senses are goodwill (see favour, goodwill) and, in the plural, thanks.

terms.gloss: given for “please do me this favour”
evidence: Traupman 98: please do me this favor, amābō tē, fac hanc grātiam mihi
terms.comment: Grātiam facere is classically to let someone off a fault or an obligation, to pardon (dēlictī grātiam facere, Sall. Jug. 104, Lewis & Short s.v. grātia; see forgive). To ask a favour, say amābō tē with the imperative, or grātum mihi fēceris, sī … (above); Terence has hanc grātiam ut sibi dēs, that you grant him this favour (Ter. Hec. 3.3.30, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: grātissimum mihi fēceris, sī ad mē in Ciliciam quam prīmum vēneris
phrases.english: you will do me the greatest favour if you come to me in Cilicia as soon as you can

phrases.latin: Inopī beneficium bis dat, quī dat celeriter.
phrases.english: He does the needy a double kindness who does it quickly.

phrases.latin: Optimē positum est beneficium, ubi ejus meminit quī accipit.
phrases.english: A kindness is best placed where the one who receives it remembers it.
to accept and return a favour
